facts.claim: AAP (Media and Young Minds, 2016): for children under 18 months, pediatricians should discourage screen media other than video chatting.

AAP: for 18 to 24 months, parents who want to introduce digital media should choose high-quality programs or apps and use them together with the child; solo media use should be avoided in this age group.
AAP: for children 2 to 5 years, limit digital media use to no more than 1 hour per day, with co-viewing recommended.
AAP recommends keeping bedrooms, mealtimes and parent-child playtime screen-free.

AAP's newer 2025 policy statement (Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents) takes a looser stance on fixed time limits: time may vary by family, needs, and school nights vs weekends, and occasional brief high-quality videos are not described as harmful. It does not replace the 2016 age bands, so the two AAP documents need to be reconciled in the copy.

AWMF S2k guideline on prevention of dysregulated screen media use in children and adolescents (version 2023-09, AWMF register no. 027-075) recommends keeping children under 3 years away from all passive and active use of screen media; the recommendation is a consensus statement (no. 25).
The AWMF guideline's parent version (2024-11) summarizes the under-3 advice as 'Bis drei: Bildschirmfrei!' (screen-free until age three).

The AWMF guideline links excessive screen use in toddlerhood to regulation and attachment disorders and to language and cognitive development, while noting that the data are described as controversial.
Kindergesundheit-info (BZgA-linked) advises that babies and toddlers under three should not watch television yet, and its age table recommends no screen media for this group.

unverified: The AWMF guideline's figure of at most 30 minutes on individual days for children from age 3, and only with a parent present, came from a secondary summary. Confirm it in the guideline text before publishing.
Whether the German guidance allows video calls for under-3s (the AAP does) is not confirmed by the sources found.
Reconciling AAP (18 to 24 months: co-viewed high-quality media allowed) with AWMF (under 3: screen-free) is an editorial decision. The English page must not claim the two agree.
The English page is ymyl and needs a named reviewer before publication; no reviewer is confirmed in this research.

facts.claim: AAP recommends a ban on the manufacture and sale of mobile infant walkers, citing data on major and minor injuries and death and no clear benefit from walkers.
AAP says stationary activity centers (no wheels) and play yards or playpens are safer alternatives to mobile baby walkers.
AAP says the vast majority of walker injuries are falls down stairs, and head injuries are common.
HealthyChildren.org says walkers do not teach children to walk and can delay walking.
AAP states that warning labels, public education, adult supervision and stair gates have not been shown to prevent walker injuries.
AAP advises that babies practice walking by cruising along furniture while a caregiver watches, and that going barefoot helps babies grip the floor with their toes.
CPSC: in 1992 an estimated 25,700 children under 15 months were treated in US emergency rooms for baby-walker injuries, most from stair falls.

CPSC voted in May 2010 to replace the old design-based federal rules with a mandatory standard (adopting ASTM F977-07 with added requirements). The standard requires walkers either to be too wide for a standard doorway or to stop at the edge of a step, so this is a standard rather than a ban.
CPSC reports an 88% reduction in walker injuries from 1994 to 2008, which it links partly to the stair-fall requirement added in the 1997 voluntary standard.

unverified: Push toy safety guidance (age, ground-contact features, handle or tip risks) was not found on any allowed official domain. The push-toy column of the comparison table cannot be sourced yet.
Whether AAP has issued a newer walker policy than the 2001 statement is unconfirmed. The HealthyChildren pages are mixed in date.
Official guidance on stationary activity centers beyond the AAP alternative statement (age limits, tip-over and stair risks) was not found.
Recalls of 2025 walkers that fail the stair-fall requirement exist (CPSC Boyro notice), but no official count for recent years was confirmed.

facts.claim: The CE mark on toys sold in the EU is a manufacturer's declaration, not an independent test mark; toys without a CE mark may not be placed on the EU market.

The GS mark indicates voluntary, independent third-party testing commissioned by the manufacturer. The additional wording 'Sicherheit und Schadstoffe' (safety and pollutants) matters for chemical safety.

Verbraucherzentrale prefers untreated solid wood; painted or lacquered wooden toys should meet the German toy standard DIN EN 71-3; plywood puzzles failed tests more often because they released formaldehyde.
Verbraucherzentrale warns that soft plastic is the bigger chemical concern: cheap no-name products may contain banned plasticizers, and polycarbonate can release bisphenol A or other bisphenols.
Kindergesundheit-info advises choosing PVC-free or phthalate-free plastic toys, with PP or PE preferred, because PVC often contains harmful plasticizers.
Kindergesundheit-info advises unpainted or waxed wood and regular checks of wooden toys for cracks, splinters and sharp edges.
CPSC limits: children's products must not exceed 100 ppm total lead in any accessible component part (for children 12 and under), and children's product paint must not exceed 90 ppm lead.

CPSC limits phthalates in children's toys and child care articles to 0.1% (1,000 ppm) per regulated phthalate in accessible component parts; untreated or unfinished wood and natural fibers are exempt from phthalate testing if not treated with a substance that may contain phthalates.

Under CPSC small-parts rules (16 CFR part 1501), toys for children under 3 must not have small parts that fit entirely in a test cylinder of about 2.25 by 1.25 inches. CPSC teether recalls in 2026 cite pull-string teethers that violate the mandatory toy standard because of choking risk.

unverified: The EN 71 toy standard content (which parts test which hazard) was not confirmed. EN 71 is not on an allowed official domain, so it needs a new source key and a primary source before use.
No new source key is defined in this research. Adding EN 71 or CE-marking explainers to Sources needs an editor decision.
Claims that wood is more durable or easier to clean than plastic, or that silicone is safer, were not found in the official sources. Do not state them as facts.
No official source ranks materials as best. The brief's table cells for durability and cleaning need a documented method or must be marked as general care advice.
Teething suitability by material was not confirmed by an official source. The CPSC teether results concern choking from pull strings and loose parts, not material choice.
Lead in teethers was not found; the CPSC search returned no teether lead warning.
